### Title
> Here begins the Roll of our most illustrious Lady, Lady Violant, Queen of Aragon, and also [the supplications] of our grace taking precedence, of the same lady's Chapel.

### Supplications

> **[Preamble]** Your humble and devoted daughter Violant, Queen of Aragon, supplicates Your Holiness that you may deign to admit the underwritten supplications to the grace of a hearing and to provide [for them] by special grace, with all opportune clauses.

> **[1. Portable Altar]** And first, [she supplicates] that Your Holiness may deign to grant to the same Queen the privilege of having a portable altar, with due reverence and honor, upon which she may have divine offices performed and celebrated by her own suitable chaplains or by any other suitable [priests], in [the usual] form and with other opportune clauses.

> **[2. Mass Before Dawn]** Likewise, [she supplicates] that the aforesaid devoted daughter of yours may be able to hear Mass and have it celebrated before dawn, [and that Your Holiness] may deign to grant [this] from the benignity, grace, and indulgence of the Apostolic See, and to impart plenary grace, with the necessary clauses.

> **[3. Confessor with Extended Faculties]** Likewise, [she supplicates] that she may, through her own confessor or any other suitable priest, whether secular or religious of whatever order, whom she shall have chosen to select, [have him] hear confessions and [that she] may be absolved of all her sins and cases whatsoever—even if they be such matters on account of which the Apostolic See ought rightly to be consulted—as often as the same [queen] has need; [and that Your Holiness] may deign to grant [this] by special grace.

> **[4. Dispensation from Fasting]** Likewise, [she supplicates] that during Lent and on other days prohibited by the Church, she may be permitted to eat meat, even if the disposition of her body does not demand it and without requiring any counsel of physicians; may [Your Holiness] deign to grant [this] as stated.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### The Queen (Regina)
The reference is almost certainly to **Violant de Bar** (1365–1431), queen consort of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). Register 2056 of ACA Cancelleria belongs to the registers of Queen Violant. She was known for her piety and active role in spiritual matters, consistent with this type of petition for extensive chapel privileges.

### Nature of the Document
This is a **rotulus** or list of petitions (*supplica*) to be presented to the papal curia. Such documents were typically drafted by the royal chancery and sent to the Crown's agents in Avignon (or later Rome) to be processed through the papal bureaucracy. The repetitive formula "concedere dignetur de gratia speciali" ("may [His Holiness] deign to grant by special grace") is standard curial language.

### Spiritual Privileges Requested
The faculties requested are typical of high-ranking medieval patrons:
- **Indulgences** for sermon attendance and *in articulo mortis* (at the moment of death)
- **Sacramental faculties** for chapel clergy independent of diocesan authority
- **Non-residence privileges** for beneficed chaplains serving the royal household
- **Absolution faculties** for *manuum iniectio* (violent assault on clergy, a reserved sin under canon law)

### Canonical Context
- The phrase "*lata per canonem*" refers to excommunication incurred automatically (*latae sententiae*) by operation of canon law
- "*In contemptum clavium*" (in contempt of the keys) refers to defiance of ecclesiastical authority; absolution was more readily granted if the offense was not committed with such contempt
- The reservation of Eucharist, matrimony, and extreme unction to diocesan clergy reflects standard canonical restrictions

Likewise, that the chaplains, the said commensals of her chapel, may recite the office of the Roman Church and not be bound to any other [rite], may [Your Holiness] deign to concede according to the general [privilege], as is evident, with [reference to] our other [letters] as above.

**[Item 3]**
Most Holy Father, to Your Holiness the lady, your devout daughter, sets forth that formerly, during the lifetime of King Peter of happy memory, her father, for certain chaplains and clerics of her chapel, commonly her commensals, a certain vow of her majesty was made—which vow was indeed issued, or rather [confirmed]—by which indifferently, as regards her said part as [well as] in the ecclesiastical forum, until the day of her death, the same chaplains and clerics could not be beneficed nor obtain any benefice. They were [so bound] and those opposing [this] seem to have [acted] commendably. From the highest [authority], since they are permitted to hold [benefices], and since concerning other [matters] they have not been able to satisfy [their obligations] according to the vow—in this matter, [difficulties] have multiplied and touched [upon many].

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

1. **Queen Violant de Bar** (c. 1365–1431): Wife of Joan I of Aragon, referred to as "devota filia vestra" (devout daughter of the Pope). She maintained a substantial household chapel and sought papal privileges for her chaplains throughout the 1380s–1390s.

2. **King Peter IV "the Ceremonious"** (1319–1387): Referred to as "Rege Petro eius patre" (King Peter, her father). This is an error or scribal confusion—Peter IV was Joan I's father, not Violant's. Violant's father was Robert I, Duke of Bar. However, in chancery rhetoric, Peter IV as her father-in-law and predecessor sovereign may be referenced in this familial manner regarding inherited privileges.

3. **Pope**: The addressee. Given the date range of the register, this would be either Urban VI (1378–1389), Boniface IX (1389–1404), or during the Avignon obedience, Clement VII (1378–1394) or Benedict XIII (1394–1423). The Crown of Aragon's shifting allegiances during the Western Schism make precise identification difficult without additional context.

### Institutional Context

- **Royal Chapel (*Capella Regia*)**: The queen's household chapel was a significant institution with its own chaplains, clerics, and liturgical requirements. The petitions here concern their ability to hold ecclesiastical benefices while serving as royal commensals.

- **Commensal Clergy**: Chaplains and clerics who ate at the queen's table ("commensales") and were part of her household. Their service to the crown often conflicted with holding regular ecclesiastical benefices.

- **Vow/Restriction**: The document references a vow made during Peter IV's lifetime restricting these clerics from obtaining benefices. This appears to have become problematic, and the queen seeks papal dispensation to allow her chaplains to hold benefices.

### Liturgical Note

- **Office of the Roman Church**: The petition that chaplains be permitted to recite the Roman Office (and not be bound to another) may relate to local Aragonese or Barcelona cathedral rites, or to obligations of specific benefices they might hold.

**Violant de Bar (Regina)**: Queen consort of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387-1396), daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. She maintained an active household and chapel, for which she sought benefices for her clerks. Her correspondence with the Avignon papacy is well documented.

**Bartomeu Çincholm[?]**: Chaplain of the queen's chapel; the surname is unusual and may be Germanic in origin or corrupted in transmission. Diocese of Valencia.

**Joan de Puig (Gerunden.)**: A scholar (young clerk in orders) of the queen's chapel, from Girona. The reference to Sant Feliu de Girona indicates a connection to that collegiate church.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

**Violant de Bar (Yolans Regina Aragonum)**
- Queen consort of Aragon (1387–1396), wife of Joan I "the Hunter"
- Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France
- Highly active in diplomacy, particularly with the Avignon papacy
- By March 1397, Joan I had died (May 1396), and Violant was queen dowager; this document may reflect her continued diplomatic activity or be a register copy of earlier correspondence

**Pope Clement VII**
- Clement VII (Robert of Geneva) was the Avignon pope (1378–1394)
- **CRITICAL NOTE**: Clement VII died on 16 September 1394. By March 1397, Benedict XIII (Pedro de Luna) had been pope at Avignon since 28 September 1394. The address to "Clementi" is therefore **anachronistic** if this document was actually composed in 1397.
- **Possible explanations**: (1) Register copy of an earlier letter with wrong date; (2) scribal error in the dating formula; (3) formulaic retention of predecessor's name

**Pere d'Artés (Petrus d'Artes)**
- Majordomo of the royal household
- Member of the noble Artés lineage of the Crown of Aragon
- Documented in other registers as a trusted envoy

**Ramon de França (Raymundus de França)**
- Doctor of decrees (canon law)
- Royal counsellor
- Likely a member of the royal chancery or an ecclesiastical legal expert

**Archbishop of Barcelona and Zaragoza**
- The text appears to reference a single prelate holding or associated with both sees
- In this period, García Fernández de Heredia was Archbishop of Zaragoza (1383–1411)
- The Archbishop of Barcelona (actually a bishopric until 1964) was unclear; this may be a conflation or error

**Antoni de Vila**
- Citizen of Barcelona seeking a canonry and prebend in Valencia
- Required dispensation for age defect (being only ~17 years old for subdiaconate/diaconate)
- Common type of papal petition from this period

### Places

- **Barcelona (Barchinone)**: Royal residence and chancery location; place of issue
- **Zaragoza (Cesarauguste)**: Capital of the Kingdom of Aragon
- **Valencia (Valentie)**: Cathedral church where the benefice was sought

### Diplomatic Context

The Crown of Aragon maintained allegiance to the Avignon papacy throughout the Western Schism. The sending of embassies with rotuli (rolls of petitions) was standard practice for obtaining graces, dispensations, and benefices from the papal curia.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

- **Violant de Bar (Yolanda of Bar)**: Queen consort of Aragon (1387-1396) as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Active in political and cultural affairs; known patron who maintained an extensive household. This rotulus is part of her efforts to secure papal benefices for her familiars.

- **Ramon d'Oliu (Raymundus de Olivo)**: Canon and dean of the cathedral of Huesca (Osca). Identified as a *bacallarius antiquus in decretis* (longstanding bachelor in canon law), indicating advanced legal education. Served as auditor and royal councillor to Joan I. His concordant election to the Huesca chapter suggests he was a compromise candidate acceptable to all parties.

- **Bernat Matheu**: Priest of Barcelona diocese seeking benefices in both Barcelona and Sogorb (Segorbe), indicating the common practice of pluralism.

- **Gerald Sengil**: A member of the queen's household (*commensalis*), whose supplication appears elsewhere in the register.

### Places

- **Osca (Huesca)**: Cathedral city in Aragon; its chapter was a significant ecclesiastical body.

- **Valencia**: The cathedral church of Valencia was one of the wealthiest in the Crown of Aragon, making its canonries highly desirable.

- **Lleida (Ilerda)**: Major cathedral city in Catalonia; site of a famous university.

- **Sogorb (Segorbe)**: Diocese in the Kingdom of Valencia, often held in union with Albarracín.

### Context

This document is a **rotulus supplicationum** or **rotulus communis**—a collective petition roll sent to the papal curia (at Avignon during the Western Schism) listing multiple individuals for whom the petitioner seeks benefices. The Crown of Aragon supported the Avignon papacy, and such rolls were a standard mechanism for royal and queenly patronage. The non obstante clauses requested papal dispensation from the usual prohibitions against holding multiple benefices (pluralism).

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Entry 1
**Item**, that to **Johan de Grau**, of the city of Vic, [be granted] a canonry with expectation of a prebend or office in the Church of Vic, and as above, in supplication of Raimund de Olivo, notwithstanding that he lacks one year of his [canonical] age, concerning which [we ask that you] deign to dispense with him, with the clauses as above.

### Entry 2
**Item**, that to **Johan Derill**, of the diocese of Lleida, [be granted] a canonry of the Church of Urgell, and as above, in supplication of Raimund de Olivo, notwithstanding that he holds in the Church of Huesca a canonry and prebend, and in the Church of Sant Pere el Vell of Huesca a certain portion, which portion he is prepared to relinquish, when and with the clauses as above.

### Entry 3
**Item**, to **Pere Pellicer**, priest of the diocese of Valencia, concerning the same, and a personatus also of Segorbe, and of the same Salvatierra, and as above, in the person of the aforesaid Raimund de Olivo, notwithstanding that he also holds a prebend of Xorcella [?] in the diocese of Valencia, and a canonry and prebend in the Church of Huesca, with the clauses as above.

### Entry 4
**Item**, to the lord **Enguarí Bonfill**, priest of the diocese of Zaragoza, a benefice to be conferred, whether with or without cure of souls, a canonry or [benefice] to become vacant of common or divided persons, at the collation of the archbishop and chapter of Tarazona, which pertains to Zaragoza, and if he is an archpriest or pleban, and that [benefice] coheres to administration or office by reason of dignity, whose fruits, without cure of a personatus, without [place of] books which can be assessed not to exceed [a certain] annual value, [we ask that you] deign to provide to the same Enguarí, notwithstanding that he is known to hold a chaplaincy without [cure] in the church of Santa Maria of the place of Rubielos, of the same diocese, with the clauses as above.

### Entry 5
**Item**, to **Raimund d'Antilles**, cleric of Valencia, born of noble lineage and studying civil law at the **studium of Montpellier**, a benefice to be conferred of a canonry also of Lleida [?], vacant or to become vacant, a dignity [which you] may provide, notwithstanding the statute regarding age, and as in the supplication above of Raimund de Olivo, notwithstanding that he does not attain the required year of his age, concerning which [we ask that you] deign to dispense, with the clauses as above.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons
- **Raimund de Olivo/Olivero**: Appears repeatedly as the principal supplicant ("in supplicatione Raymundi de Olivo"). Likely a proctor or agent at the papal curia presenting multiple petitions on behalf of Aragonese clerics.
- **Johan de Grau**: Petitioner for a canonry at Vic; requires age dispensation.
- **Johan Derill**: Cleric of Lleida seeking benefice at Urgell; already holds positions at Huesca, including at **Sant Pere el Vell** (the old Romanesque cathedral).
- **Pere Pellicer**: Valencian priest with existing benefices in Valencia (possibly Xorcella, unidentified locality) and Huesca.
- **Enguarí Bonfill**: Priest of Zaragoza diocese seeking benefice under Tarazona's collation; holds chaplaincy at **Rubielos** (likely Rubielos de Mora, Teruel).
- **Raimund d'Antilles**: Valencian noble studying at **Montpellier** – a major studium generale for law in the Crown of Aragon's sphere. The Montpellier connection is significant given its acquisition by France in 1349 but continued Aragonese academic ties.

### Places
- **Vic (Vicus)**: Episcopal see in Catalonia
- **Urgell**: Episcopal see in the Pyrenees
- **Huesca (Osca)**: Aragonese episcopal see; **Sant Pere el Vell** is the old cathedral
- **Segorbe**: Episcopal see in Valencia
- **Tarazona (Tirasona)**: Episcopal see in Aragon
- **Rubielos (de Mora)**: Town in Teruel, diocese of Zaragoza/Teruel
- **Montpellier**: The studium is explicitly mentioned – important for Crown of Aragon students despite French sovereignty

### Documentary Context
This folio forms part of a **rotulus** or collection of supplications being prepared for submission to the papal curia, likely during negotiations for benefice provisions. The formula "cum clausulis ut supra" indicates standardized petition language established earlier in the register.

### Persons

- **Violant de Bar (Queen):** Wife of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). In 1381, Joan was still Infante/Duke of Girona; his father Pere III (the Ceremonious) was king. If this dating is correct, Violant was acting in some official capacity, possibly during Pere III's illness or absence. Alternatively, there may be a dating issue.

- **Romeu (Bishop of Lleida):** This likely refers to **Romeu Sescomes** (Bishop of Lleida 1361–1380) or his successor. Romeu Sescomes was a notable figure who attended the Council of Tarragona and was involved in various ecclesiastical and political matters. His authorship of a treatise on *desfer maleficis* (undoing harmful magic/spells) is extremely interesting for the history of magic and demonology in the medieval Crown of Aragon.

- **Johan de Pobla:** Doctor in decrees (canon law) and citizen of Lleida; likely a legal official or academic at the studium of Lleida who had custody of the bishop's book.

- **Bishop of Tortosa:** In 1381, this would be **Guillem de Torrelles** (bishop 1369–1379) or **Hug de Llupià** (bishop 1379–1397). The sequestration of his goods suggests serious accusations or royal displeasure—possibly related to political conflict, debt, or ecclesiastical discipline.

- **Francesc ça Rel:** Royal scribe/notary of the Queen's chancery.

### Places

- **Zaragoza:** Capital of the Kingdom of Aragon; site of ecclesiastical councils and royal residence.
- **Lleida:** Important city with a cathedral chapter and university (studium generale); center of legal and theological learning.
- **Barcelona:** Capital of the Principality of Catalonia; usual seat of royal chancery.
- **Tortosa:** Diocese in southern Catalonia, economically and strategically significant.

### Subjects

- **Maleficia and the book on "desfer maleficis":** This is a significant reference to a medieval treatise on combating harmful magic. The Queen's urgent need for such a book suggests either a case of suspected witchcraft at court, illness attributed to maleficium, or scholarly/legal interest. This fits the broader context of growing concern with magic and witchcraft in late 14th-century Iberia.

- **Sequestration of episcopal goods:** Royal sequestration of a bishop's temporal goods was a serious measure, typically indicating either vacancy sede vacante, suspected treason, major debt, or conflict between crown and bishop. The involvement of both King and Queen, with instructions to the Governor of Aragon, suggests a matter of high political importance.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon, wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Known for her political acumen and extensive correspondence. These letters date from the final weeks of Joan I's reign—he would die on 19 May 1396 while hunting, making the June date potentially problematic (see uncertainties below).

**Joan I of Aragon** (1350–1396): Called "el Caçador" (the Hunter). King of Aragon 1387–1396. Died without surviving male issue on 19 May 1396, succeeded by his brother Martí I.

**Charles III of Navarre** (1361–1425): Called "the Noble." King of Navarre 1387–1425. Cousin to the Aragonese royal family through multiple lines. The familiar address "molt car cosí" reflects genuine kinship.

**Ramon de Vilanova**: Alguatzir (bailiff/marshal) of the royal household, a position of considerable trust involving enforcement of royal justice and household security.

**Mossèn Ramon d'Abella**: A Catalan nobleman evidently in disfavor with the Crown. The reference to his "lineage" posing a threat to the king suggests he may have been connected to rival claimants or factions. The Abella family held lands in the Pallars region.

**Petrus de Besanta (Pere de Besanta)**: Royal scribe of the Queen's chancery. The subscriptions identify him as the writer of both documents.

**Jacobus Castell**: A chaplain of the Queen's household who authorized the first document (ad relationem).

### Places

**Barcelona**: Primary seat of the Crown of Aragon's administration in this period; the royal chancery operated from here.

### Chronological Problem

The date of **June 1396** is problematic because Joan I died on **19 May 1396**. If these documents are accurately dated, they would have been issued during the brief interregnum or the Queen may have continued to use her title during the transition. Alternatively, there may be an error in the year reading. The "primº" after the year in the first document (indicating regnal year) is unusual if the king had already died.

### Persons
- **La Reyna / The Queen**: Almost certainly **Violant de Bar** (c. 1365–1431), Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). She was active in chancery affairs, particularly regarding household and financial matters. Register 2056 belongs to her series.

### Dating Problem (Document 2)
The date "mil ccc lxxx" (1380) in Document 2 is problematic because:
1. Violant de Bar only married Joan I in 1380 and would not yet have had active chancery registers

**Probable explanation**: Either a scribal error in the date (perhaps omitting "vij" for 1387), or this is a copy of an earlier document (possibly from Queen Sibil·la de Fortià, d. 1406, fourth wife of Pere III) inserted into Violant's register.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document A

**The Queen**

Justice: We have sent once to Johan don Sanxo by our letter [carried by] Guerau de Plaça, our candle-keeper [*candelent*], to bring a chapel [vestment or chapel object/cap] which is worth twenty-four gold florins. And the said Johan has not wished to release nor deliver the said chapel to the said Guerau, alleging some frivolous reasons, to which we cannot give credence, saying that because the Lord King had not given him a written agreement [*capitulat*] concerning the things he was owed, he was retaining the said chapel; and [we say] that for a debt that the Lord King [owes] him, he has no right to retain this one [item].

Wherefore, since we had designated that the said chapel should have been delivered throughout the month of April most recently passed, and the said Johan had departed, and to deliver it [we] send again the said Guerau to demand and obtain the same, to whom we have entrusted certain words on our behalf to say to you:

For which reason we ask and command you, giving faith to what the said Guerau will explain to you on our behalf, just as if we ourselves said it, [that you] fulfil that by deed, with constraint and force, according as we trust in you. Certifying to us that the delay in obtaining the said chapel is to us most displeasing.

Given in Barcelona on the 26th of June of the year of [Our Lord] 1383. The Queen.

**[Address:]** To our beloved Mossèn Domingo de Muy, chaplain of the Lord King and Justice of Aragon.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

1. **Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431)**: Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I. Active in administration of the royal household and frequently issued mandates under her own authority, particularly regarding household goods, debts, and ecclesiastical affairs. Her register (2056) is a key source for queenly agency in the late medieval Crown of Aragon.

2. **Domingo de Muy**: Identified as both royal chaplain (*capellero del Senyor Rey*) and Justice of Aragon (*Justicia Daragon*). If this identification is correct, this is highly significant. The Justice of Aragon was a major constitutional officer who adjudicated disputes between the Crown and subjects. However, I find no corroboration of a "Domingo de Muy" as Justice; the Justice in 1383 was **Domingo Cerdán** (in office 1362–1389). This may be a variant spelling or a confusion with a subordinate official in the Justice's household.

3. **Johan don Sanxo**: A creditor or artisan holding an item (the *capell*) as security for a debt owed by the Crown. His retention of goods against royal demands illustrates ongoing tensions over royal creditworthiness.

4. **Guerau de Plaça**: A household officer (*candelent* — keeper of candles/wax, a minor household position) employed as a messenger and agent for debt recovery.

5. **P. de Besanta**: Royal secretary (*scriptor*) active in Violant's chancery. The same hand and subscription appears on both documents.

6. **Francesc Çarandera**: General Procurator (*procurador general*) of the Queen, a senior legal officer managing her estates and judicial affairs. His *visa* indicates the letter passed through proper administrative review.

### Objects

- **Capell**: The term typically means "cap" or "hood" but in this context likely refers either to a liturgical vestment (a cope or chapel furnishing) or an item of precious headwear valued at 24 gold florins — a substantial sum (roughly equivalent to several months' wages for a skilled craftsman).

### Places

- **Barcelona (Barçina / Barchinona)**: The royal court was frequently resident in Barcelona during Joan I's reign.

### Dating Issue

- Document B's date "xxx dies de ffebrer" (30 February) is impossible. February 1388 had 29 days (1388 was a leap year). This may be:
  - Scribal error for "xxviij" (28) or "xx" (20)
  - Error for March ("març")
  - The scribe's confusion in a late-registered entry

Most dear Uncle, because we are desirous of knowing your health and wellbeing, we pray you affectionately that you be willing to write to us at the soonest moment that can be done. And because we know you will take pleasure from it, we certify to you that the lord King, our lord and husband, we ourselves, and our daughters are in good health and wellbeing, by the mercy of our lord God.

Most dear Uncle, we have learned that in your duchy and counties a great assembly of men-at-arms is being made with the enterprise of entering the realms and lands of the said lord King to damage them and their subjects (?). ### Document A: To the Duchess of Brittany

**[Folio 108]**

To our very dear cousin: We have received your letter, from which we have had supreme pleasure as we have learned of your estate and health, and of the deliverance of [your] fair son that God has given us [i.e., to our family/lineage]. Afterwards, since we know that you will take pleasure in it, we notify you that the lord King, our lord and husband, we ourselves, and our daughters are in good estate of health, by the mercy of God. We pray you that as often as may be done, you certify us of your estate. Be assured that we shall have very great pleasure therein, and we shall greatly [appreciate] it.

Moreover, very dear cousin, because we have understood through certain notices that have come from those parts by way of Brittany and other places—[namely] that this way of life [continues]—for indeed the Duke of Brittany is making an assembly of men-at-arms and an enterprise to enter the realms of the said lord [King] and to damage them in aid of the Count of Armagnac, and that [this is happening] notwithstanding [his obligation to] regard the duty of blood and bond of good friendship that exists between the said Duke, our husband, and us, and you—

Wherefore, very dear cousin, we pray you affectionately that, wishing to consider the good friendship and cordial affection that the said lord King and we have had at all times and have today toward your House, and the duty of blood, [that] you would cause the said assembly to cease and end the said enterprise [and dismiss] the said companies, in such manner that the said Count, by force of your promises, may not be able to offend or do any damage to the realms and territories of the said lord.

And for this the said lord King and we shall thank you and consider ourselves more obligated to do you all honors and pleasures. And if any things, very dear cousin, please you properly that we may do for you, frankly inform us of them, for we shall do them most willingly. May the Holy Spirit be at all times your guide. Given at Barcelona under our seal [by order of the provost?]. [Day] of January of the year 1390. The Queen.

**[Subscription]:** The Queen of Aragon

**[To]:** Our very dear cousin the Duchess of Brittany, Countess of Montfort and of Richmond.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolanda de Bar), Queen of Aragon (c. 1365–1431)**
Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France (daughter of King Jean II of France). She married the Infante Joan of Aragon (future Joan I) in 1380. Queen consort from 1387 until Joan I's death in 1396. A highly cultured figure, patron of letters, and active in diplomacy, particularly maintaining ties with France.

**Joan I of Aragon ("el Caçador" / "l'Amador de la gentilesa") (1350–1396)**
King of Aragon, Valencia, Majorca, Sardinia, and Corsica; Count of Barcelona. Succeeded his father Pere IV (Pere el Cerimoniós) in 1387. Known for his devotion to music, poetry, and hunting.

**Mossèn Ponç de Perellos**
A Catalan nobleman. The Perellos (Perellós) family held lordships in Roussillon. Ponç de Perellos served the Crown of Aragon in diplomatic capacities. The famous "Viatge al Purgatori de Sant Patrici" (1398) was authored by Ramon de Perellos, a relative and prominent figure at Joan I's court.

**Charles VI, King of France ("le Bien-Aimé" / "le Fol") (1368–1422)**
King of France from 1380. Nephew of Violant de Bar (his mother, Jeanne de Bourbon, was a cousin of Violant's). The familial relationship explains the warmth of the letter and the address "frare" (brother).

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

**Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon, wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie de France. A significant political figure and patron of the arts; these letters document her regular correspondence with her natal family in Bar.

**Joan I of Aragon** ("lo senyor Rey senyor e marit"): King of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). Known as "the Hunter" (el Caçador). His health was a matter of diplomatic importance.

**Marie de France, Duchess of Bar** ("ma cara mare e senyora la senyera Duquessa de Bar"): Violant's mother, daughter of King Jean II of France. The title "senyora" used here is deferential; the unusual "senyera" appears to be a scribal error for "senyora."

**Robert I, Duke of Bar** ("Duci de Bar"): Violant's father, recipient of a parallel letter noted in the Latin chancery annotation.

**Philip of Bar** ("moss[en] Philip de Bar"): Violant's brother. The honorific "mossèn" indicates his noble status. He was a younger son of the Duke of Bar.

**Lostin de Sant Martí**: A messenger or envoy entrusted with letters and, significantly, with oral instructions ("de algunes coses que deu a vos parlar"). This practice of combining written letters with oral messages was standard in medieval diplomacy.

**"Nostres filles"**: The infantas Joana (b. 1382) and Violant (b. 1384), daughters of Violant and Joan I.

### Diplomatic Observations

These are formulaic *littere clause* (sealed letters) of the type routinely sent by queens to maintain family relations. The "sanitat de sanitat" formula (health news) was a conventional component of late medieval correspondence. The letters demonstrate the use of the secret seal ("sag[ue]ll secret") for personal correspondence, distinct from the great seal used for official acts.

The Latin notation "Fuit alia similis missa..." is a standard register annotation indicating duplicate correspondence — essential for maintaining chancery records.

**Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431)**: Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. The reference to **Venetian galleys** carrying English cloth from Flanders reflects the Mediterranean trade routes of the late fourteenth century. The *muda* system of Venetian state-organized galley convoys regularly connected the eastern Mediterranean with Flanders, carrying luxury goods including textiles.

**Cafiz/cafís**: A dry measure for grain, varying by region. In Aragon, approximately 140–200 liters. Two thousand cafices would represent a substantial grain shipment, likely for provisioning or sale.

Wherefore we humbly beseech Your Beatitude to deign to ensure [?] that procurations by the said Viscount for the aforesaid [marriage] expenses, and to the same [envoy] or others [?] for the aforesaid [matter], [that] audience be denied, since, Holy Father, this seems necessary to [Your] Apostolic [Holiness] and to religion, and would be the cause of destruction of a capital [sin?] of the said Viscount, which is wondrous and notable in many ways in the royal dominion of this kind [of kingdom].

[May Your Holiness] deign graciously to nurture [this matter] most fully for prosperous and long-lasting times.

Given at Vilafranca del Penedès on the last day of November in the year of the Nativity of the Lord one thousand three hundred and ninety-one.

- Jaufre VI de Rocabertí (d. 1403), powerful noble of the County of Empúries. The Rocabertí viscounts held extensive territories in northern Catalonia near the French border. This marriage dispute is documented in other ACA registers as a significant canonical controversy.

**Joan I of Aragon (Johannes dei gratia Rex Aragonum)**
- Known as "the Hunter" (el Caçador), reigned 1387–1396. Son of Pere III (the Ceremonious). His reign saw continued financial difficulties inherited from his father's military campaigns, reflected in the second document's discussion of patrimonial alienations.

**Pere III of Aragon (Petrus Rex Aragonum patrem nostrum memorie gloriose)**
- Pere III "the Ceremonious" (1319–1387), whose extensive military expenditures (Sardinia, Castile, Mallorca reconquest) had severely depleted the royal patrimony, necessitating subsidies from the Corts and municipal councils.

### Places Identified

**Vilafranca del Penedès (villafrancha penitensi)**
- Important town in Catalonia, frequent location of royal and municipal assemblies. The date (30 November 1391) places this document shortly after the major anti-Jewish violence of August 1391.

**Lleida/Lérida (Jlerde/Jherde)**
- Major city of western Catalonia, seat of an important bishopric and studium generale (university). The city's involvement suggests municipal opposition to the Rocabertí marriage, possibly due to interests in the Exèrica inheritance or religious considerations.

### Historical Context

The document reflects several intersecting concerns of the 1390s:

1. **Canonical marriage disputes**: The allegation that Elionor had taken solemn religious vows would make any subsequent marriage invalid under canon law. Such cases required papal dispensation or adjudication.

2. **Municipal-noble tensions**: The city of Lleida's intervention suggests possible economic or political interests in preventing the Rocabertí-Exèrica alliance, which would have consolidated significant noble holdings.

3. **Crown finances under Joan I**: The second document reflects ongoing negotiations between the Crown and municipal councils (consells) regarding subsidies to offset the patrimony's depletion under Pere III.

### Persons Identified:

1. **Violant de Bar (Yolanda of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. Known for her cultural patronage and political influence. The spelling "Volant" reflects Catalan orthographic conventions.

2. **Ramon Alamany de Cervelló** (fl. 1380s–1410s): Major Catalan nobleman (*miles*), serving as *Camarlenc* (Chamberlain) to Joan I and as *Governador General de Catalunya*. The Cervelló family held extensive lordships in the Penedès region. His role as Governor made him effectively the king's chief representative in Catalonia.

3. **Berenguer de Cornellà** (*Bergario de Cornyllo*): Royal Treasurer (*Thesaurarius*) under Joan I. Responsible for disbursements from the royal fisc.

4. **Huc d'Anglesola**: Member of the prominent Anglesola lineage of Urgell. The reference to "obra nouellament feta" (newly made construction) at Tàrrega and disputed privileges suggests a local conflict over seigneurial rights or fortification, common in this period.

5. **Sabat d'Appoli / Viscount of Roda**: The Viscount of Roda (Ribagorça) was a title held by a cadet branch of the counts of Pallars. "Sabat d'Appoli" may be a rendering of a compound name; requires further identification.

6. **"de Besanta"**: The scribe responsible for the document's redaction. Likely a member of the Queen's secretariat.

### Historical Context:

The date (June 1392) places this document in the middle of Joan I's reign, a period marked by:
- Ongoing fiscal pressures from the costs of maintaining royal government
- The importance of the Catalan nobility in royal administration
- Violant de Bar's active role in governance, including issuing documents under her own authority (*Nos Volant dei gratia*)

The grant of 6,000 Aragonese gold florins to the Governor of Catalonia represents a substantial sum, reflecting both the importance of the office and the personal services rendered. Such grants (*gràcies*) were a key mechanism for maintaining noble loyalty.

### First Document

**For the same Porta, second [payment], disbursed**

We, Joan, and we, Violant, etc. In partial remuneration of the labors sustained by you, our faithful Arnau Porta of our Treasury of the King, and Pere Civada of our Treasury of the said Queen, in present and past matters as guarantors for those who have exchanged [currency for] our Call of the City of Barcelona—let them give gold florins of Aragon, namely to each of you five hundred—we give and graciously grant to you by these presents. By which we command our faithful Julià Garriu, our Treasurer of the said King, and Bernat de Castella, our Treasurer of the said Queen, that from the monies which from our compositions especially and those to be executed shall come or shall have come to their hands, the said Julià shall give to you, the said Arnau, one thousand five hundred *tabulas* [accounting units] and shall pay out in such payment as they shall see fit to make to you until the deduction [is complete], to you with a receipt of payment.

In witness whereof we have ordered the present [letters] to be made and fortified with our seal. Given in the Monastery of Santa Eulàlia de Valldoreix, the third day of October in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1390. By the Lord King. Seen by Pere de Beneficis.

### Second Document

**For Spant de Cardona**

Let it be evident to all who shall inspect the page of this charter:

¶ We, Joan, by the grace of God King of Aragon, etc., and we, Violant, by the same grace Queen of Aragon and Countess of the County of [?], consort of the said King:

It befits every King and royal dignity that those whom abundant commended service renders worthy, and not inconsiderable affection of services and prompt [devotion] makes pleasing to their royal and queenly goodwill, [the Crown] should prefer with many and numerous preliminary graces, so that others may be encouraged to follow and to well-deserved merits.

Because we have duly and attentively received into our regard the living, grateful, and acceptable services rendered by you, our faithful councillor and promoter of the affairs of our Court of the Lord King, **Spant de Cardona, jurist**, for not a few years before we were elevated to the heights of kingdom and rule, and also afterward rendered—not without personal effort and the sweat and expenditure of your resources—[we deem you] worthy of a more ample grace as described below.

By the tenor of this present [document], with this respect holding force for us and our successors and our [heirs], and from certain knowledge and spontaneous will and also by our own motion, in partial remuneration of the aforesaid [services], we grant, confer, and donate by pure, perfect, and notable donation *inter vivos* to you, the noble said Spant of the aforesaid Cardona, and to your [heirs] in perpetuity, as free, own, and franc allod:

**The Major Synagogue or School of the Call Major that the Jews of the City of Barcelona [possess]**, with all appurtenances, all buildings, constructions, appendages, boundaries, and all pertinences of the said synagogue or major school, from the top to the bottom, and with all the census payments, revenues, and all rights which are or have been owed to the same synagogue or its rector for the same, by whomsoever; as well as with all and total other right [acquired] by us or either of us on account of the dissolution of the aljama of the Jews and of the aforesaid Call, or the school, or over the same synagogue or school and the other aforesaid [properties], howsoever acquired.

This concession and donation we have indeed made to you, the said Spant of the aforesaid Cardona, and to your [heirs] in perpetuity, concerning the synagogue or school and the other aforesaid [properties], freely and absolutely—

1. **Eviction Warranty (euinccio/evictio)**: This is an extensive eviction guarantee clause standard in Crown of Aragon royal sales. ### Persons Identified

1. **Pere Olzina de Berga** (Petrus Olzina de Berga): The beneficiary of this grant. He appears to be receiving rights or jurisdiction over the synagogue/school of the Barcelona Jewish Call. This may relate to the complex situation of Jewish property and institutional rights in late 14th-century Barcelona, particularly after the anti-Jewish violence of the 1390s (though this document predates the 1391 pogrom by three years).

2. **Queen Violant de Bar** (Yolande of Bar, 1365–1431): Queen consort of Joan I of Aragon. The document's reference to "excellentissimi domini Regis viri et domini mei carissimi" (the most excellent lord King, my husband and my dearest lord) confirms this is issued by Violant in her queenly capacity. Violant was known to have her own chancery and issued documents regarding Jewish communities.

3. **Felip de França / Guillem Burguets / Jaume Patropí**: These appear to be royal officials or administrators connected to the Barcelona Jewish Call. "França" may indicate French origin or a toponym.

4. **The Barcelona Call (Calle judeorum civitatis Barchinone)**: The Jewish quarter of Barcelona, one of the most important Jewish communities in medieval Iberia. By 1388, the community was under increasing pressure, just three years before its destruction in the 1391 massacres.

- **Sinagoga seu scola aljame**: The synagogue or school of the aljama. In medieval Iberian Jewish communities, the "scola" often referred to the synagogue as a place of study and prayer. The document appears to concern the transfer of certain rights over this institution.

- **The date of 4 December 1388** places this document in the reign of **Joan I** (r. 1387–1396). The regnal situation is notable: Joan I had succeeded Pere III (IV) in January 1387, and Violant de Bar had become queen consort.

### Register Context

This document is found in ACA Cancelleria, Registros, núm. 2056, which is part of the registers of **Violant de Bar**. This confirms the queenly origin of the mandate.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### San Juan de la Peña (*Sanctus Johannes de la Penya / Sant Joan de la Penya*)
The Royal Monastery of San Juan de la Peña, located in the Aragonese Pyrenees near Jaca, was one of the most important monasteries of the Crown of Aragon. Founded in the 10th century, it served as the royal pantheon for early Aragonese kings and held exceptional significance as a symbol of Aragonese identity. The kings of Aragon held patronage rights (*ius patronatus*) over the monastery, as explicitly stated in this document ("nos patroni sumus").

### Joan de Nogario / Noguera
The individual nominated as abbot. The title *Claviger maior* (Major Claustral or Senior Key-keeper) indicates he held a senior administrative position in the monastery before this nomination. This was typically the second-ranking official after the abbot.

### Bishop of Tarazona
The Diocese of Tarazona held jurisdiction over ecclesiastical matters in this region of Aragon. The bishop's cooperation was necessary for the confirmation of abbatial elections, particularly in cases where royal patronage intersected with canonical procedures.

### Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387-1396)
King Joan I "el Caçador" (the Hunter) was actively involved in ecclesiastical appointments throughout his reign. His exercise of patronage rights over San Juan de la Peña reflects the ongoing royal interest in controlling this symbolically important institution.

### Pere de Beçanta
A chancery official (*scriptor*) serving under Joan I. His name appears in the standard subscription formula indicating that the document was produced on royal mandate through his office.

### Date Context: November 1394
This document falls during a period of relative stability in Joan I's reign, before the crises of 1395-1396 that would culminate in his sudden death in May 1396.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document A

**The Queen**

Since for the benefit of the governance and administration of that aljama we desire someone capable [?], and we have deliberated that for this purpose good [men] would be Salamo Abnarrabi or his son, who understand and know the affairs of the said aljama—therefore we tell you and expressly command you that the said Salamo or his son, or some other person in whom you can well trust, you shall send to us immediately and without delay with sufficient power [of attorney] from the said aljama. And in this you shall place no delay whatsoever if you desire to serve us well. Provided however that he whom you send [shall arrive] before us within eight days of [receiving] this present letter. Given in Barcelona under our privy seal on the 26th day of February of the year 1395, on the flat [i.e., sealed flat rather than pendant].

**[Address]:** To the Adelantados and Aljama of the Jews of the City of Zaragoza

**[Scribal note]:** On behalf of Bernat, by mandate of the Lady Queen; Guillem Ponç drafted it.

### Document B

Most high and most excellent prince and powerful lord, husband and lord of ours, most dear, with fullest [expression of devotion], I supplicate your lordship that it may please your mercy to grant, give, transfer, and release graciously to mossèn Antoni de Vilaragut all rights and claims pertaining to your lordship for whatever reason and case in the properties which belonged to the late Pere de Busquets, citizen of the city of Valencia—of which [properties] the said Pere made a donation to mossèn Bernat d'Aprera, [naming him] as third [heir/beneficiary?] among those of the said city, and of which [properties] the said Pere instituted as his heir in his last testament the said mossèn Antoni, notwithstanding the said donation made to the said mossèn Bernat, as appears in the said last testament of the said Pere. And this, lord, I would consider a singular grace toward your lordship, whom may our Lord exalt for many years. Written in Barcelona on the 26th day of February of the year 1395.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (1365–1431):** Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I, daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. Known for her active role in governance and her own chancery. Register 2056 belongs to her personal registers (*Reginae Yolantis*).

**Joan I of Aragon (1350–1396):** King of Aragon 1387–1396, nicknamed *el Caçador* (the Hunter). Husband of Violant de Bar from 1380.

**Salamo Abnarrabi (Šelomoh ibn al-Rabī):** A prominent member of the Jewish community of Zaragoza. The family name *Abnarrabi* (from Arabic *ibn al-rabī*) indicates descent from a rabbinic lineage. Jewish communal representatives were frequently summoned to the royal court on fiscal and administrative matters.

**Antoni de Vilaragut:** A Valencian noble family; several members named Antoni appear in late 14th-century documents. The Vilaraguts were involved in the baronial conflicts of the period.

**Pere de Busquets:** A citizen (*ciutadà*) of Valencia, deceased by 1395. His estate became the subject of competing claims between a donation *inter vivos* to Bernat d'Aprera and a testamentary institution naming Antoni de Vilaragut as heir.

**Bernat d'Aprera:** Likely a Valencian notable; recipient of a donation from Pere de Busquets that was later superseded or contested by the testament.

### Institutions

### Persons
- **Marquis of Villena**: Alfonso of Aragon, Marquis of Villena (1332-1412), first cousin of Pere III of Aragon. Held extensive lordships in Valencia and Castile. His conflicts with the Crown over Moorish vassals (mudéjars) were frequent in this period.

- **Antoni Vendrell**: Local batlle (royal bailiff) of Valguerra. The Vendrell family was prominent in the Penedès region.

- **Pere de Besanta**: Royal scribe (scriptor) active in the chancery during this period. His name appears in subscription formulae.

### Places
- **Vall d'Agora / Vall d'Aiora**: Valley in the Kingdom of Valencia, near the Castilian border. Area with significant mudéjar population under various lordships.

- **Valguerra**: Likely Vallguarnera or a variant spelling of a Valencian locality.

- **Vilafranca de Penedès**: Major town in Catalonia where the royal court frequently resided; seat of an important royal curia.

- **Pont Saborny**: Possibly Pont de Suert or another bridge crossing; location uncertain.

### Context
The document concerns the complex jurisdictional disputes over mudéjar (Muslim) vassals between the Crown, the Queen's personal lordships, and magnates like the Marquis of Villena. The Queen maintained personal authority over certain Moorish communities, and their seizure by other lords constituted a violation of her rights.

**Elionor d'Arborea (c. 1340–1404)**
The "Jutgessa d'Arborea" addressed in the first letter is Eleonora d'Arborea, one of the most significant figures in Sardinian history. She was the de facto ruler of the Giudicato of Arborea, the last independent Sardinian state resisting Aragonese conquest. She promulgated the *Carta de Logu*, a legal code that remained in force until 1827. The address "molt cara cosina" reflects the diplomatic fiction of kinship used in royal correspondence, though there were distant family connections through the Aragonese royal house.

**Violant de Bar (1365–1431)**
The issuing queen, wife of Joan I of Aragon. As queen consort, she maintained her own chancery and household, issuing documents under her privy seal (*segell privat*). She was notably active in cultural patronage and political affairs.

**Açtal de Lunhayres**
A member of the queen's household or an agent recommended to the Sardinian court. The name "Lunhayres" (possibly Linyares/Llunaires) suggests Occitan or Catalan origin.

**Abbot of Bages / Sant Joan de la Pera**
The second letter concerns a contested abbatial election, likely at Sant Joan de les Abadesses or a related monastery. The reference to "Bages" likely refers to Sant Benet de Bages, a Benedictine monastery. These ecclesiastical disputes over collation rights (the right to appoint to benefices) were common in this period.

**Barcelona**: The court's location when these letters were issued.

**Cort de Roma**: The papal court, at this time in Rome (the Western Schism was ongoing, with rival popes in Rome and Avignon; the Crown of Aragon supported the Avignon obedience under Clement VII until 1394, then Benedict XIII).

The date (March 1395) places these documents during the reign of Joan I (r. 1387–1396), during a period of complex relations with Sardinia (ongoing warfare and negotiation with the Giudicato of Arborea) and ecclesiastical politics (the Western Schism).

February 1395 falls during a period of increasing royal preoccupation with Sardinian affairs, Gascon diplomacy (given Violant's French connections), and internal administration. ## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. Known for her cultural patronage and political activity. After Joan I's death in May 1396, she faced conflicts with his successor Martí I over her dower lands. This document dates from two months before Joan's death.

**Ramon Boïl**: Governor (*Governador* or *Portantveus de Governador*) of the Kingdom of Valencia. The Boïl family was a prominent Valencian noble lineage. He served as the crown's chief judicial and administrative officer in the kingdom.

**Vescomte de Vilanova (Viscount of Vilanova)**: Likely a member of the Vilanova lineage holding this viscounty. The family held lands in Catalonia and Valencia.

**Jaume Ximeno**: Identified as a "moço" (servant/young man) of Valencia; party to the lawsuit.

**Petrus de Besanta**: Scribe in Queen Violant's chancery. The formula "Domina Regina mandavit mihi" is standard for documents issued under the queen's authority.

### Context

Document 1 concerns a **civil lawsuit** between a viscount and a commoner being heard before the Governor's court in Valencia. The Queen intervenes to ensure swift justice without procedural delays—a common concern in medieval litigation where parties could use dilatory tactics indefinitely.

Document 2 is an **order for luxury goods** (possibly textiles or decorative items) from a Moorish supplier in Valencia. The Valencian *morería* (Muslim quarter) was renowned for its craftsmen, particularly in textiles, ceramics, and luxury goods. The queen's direct correspondence with a Muslim artisan/merchant reflects the integrated economic role of *mudéjars* (Muslims under Christian rule) in the Crown of Aragon.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

1. **La Reyna Daragon / The Queen of Aragon**: Almost certainly **Violant de Bar** (1365–1431), wife of King Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). The register date of 1395 and address to Pope Benedict XIII confirm this identification. Violant was politically active and maintained her own chancery correspondence.

2. **Pope Benedict XIII**: Pedro Martínez de Luna (c. 1328–1423), the Avignon pope of the Western Schism, elected 28 September 1394. The Crown of Aragon recognized the Avignon obedience. The address "Benedicto... summo pontifici" confirms this is post-September 1394.

3. **En Bernat Metge**: Likely the celebrated Catalan author **Bernat Metge** (c. 1340/46–1413), who served as secretary to Joan I and Violant de Bar. Author of *Lo Somni* (1399). His presence as recipient of a royal letter concerning monastic affairs is consistent with his role as a senior chancery official.

4. **Monastery of Sant Jeroni**: The document concerns a **Hieronymite (Jeronymite) monastery** in the diocese of Barcelona. This is likely **Sant Jeroni de la Murtra** (founded 1416) or more probably **Sant Jeroni de la Vall d'Hebron** (founded 1393), which was being endowed during this exact period. The request to convert rectories into vicarages and unite their revenues to the monastery is a standard method of monastic endowment.

### Historical Context

- The Western Schism (1378–1417) divided European allegiance between Rome and Avignon. The Crown of Aragon supported the Avignon line.
- Violant de Bar was known for her cultural patronage and administrative involvement. Her letters often addressed ecclesiastical and diplomatic matters directly.
- The Hieronymite Order was expanding rapidly in Iberia during the late 14th century under royal patronage.

### Persons Identified or Potentially Identifiable:

1. **"La Reyna" (Doc. A, 1388)**: Given the date April 1388, this is almost certainly **Sibil·la de Fortià** (c. 1350–1406), fourth wife of Pere III "el Cerimoniós," who died in January 1387. However, Joan I's queen **Violant de Bar** was also active by this date. The register number (2056) would need verification against known attributions.

2. **"Regina Aragonum" (Doc. B)**: The Latin formulation and references to papal provisions strongly suggest **Violant de Bar** (1365–1431), queen consort of Joan I (r. 1387–1396), known for extensive correspondence with the Avignon papacy during the Western Schism.

3. **Jacobus de Caponibus**: Possibly identifiable with the **Capons/Caponys** family, known in Barcelona patriciate and royal service.

4. **Duardus Aquilano/Aquilos**: A royal familiar seeking ecclesiastical benefice; the name suggests possible Italian origin or connection.

5. **"Cardinalis pro Auguste"**: Reference to a Cardinal associated with the see of **Vic** (Augusta in Latin) or possibly **Augsburg**. This vacancy would help date the document precisely if identified.

6. **The Papal Context**: References to the "Summus Pontifex" during this period indicate the **Avignon Pope** (Clement VII, 1378–1394, or Benedict XIII, 1394–1423), given the Crown of Aragon's adherence to the Avignon obedience during the Western Schism.

### Institutional Context:

The document reflects the system of **papal provisions** and **expectative graces** whereby royal households sought benefices for their servants through papal favor—a major feature of late medieval ecclesiastical politics and a source of tension between secular rulers and the papacy.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

- **La Reyna / La Reyna d'Aragó**: Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar), queen consort of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). She was politically active and maintained her own chancery correspondence. Documents from her register survive in ACA Cancelleria.

- **Guillelmus de Besanta**: Chancery official who validated documents with the formula "visa per me in consilio" (seen by me in council). Active in the 1390s.

- **Mossèn [?]rano Sabella, Governor of Mallorca**: The reading of the first name is uncertain. The office of Governor (*Governador*) of Mallorca was a royal appointment overseeing the island's administration.

- **Bishop of Tarragona**: In 1395, this was Ènnec de Vallterra (Íñigo de Vallterra), archbishop 1387–1407.

- **El Portell**: Likely a locality; there are several places of this name in the Crown of Aragon. The context suggests a jurisdictional or ecclesiastical dispute.

- **Mallorca**: The Kingdom of Mallorca (reincorporated into the Crown of Aragon in 1349) remained administratively distinct under its own governor.

- **Guardiamatge del port de la mar**: The office of maritime port guardianship, concerned with harbor administration, customs, and maritime defense.

### Offices

- **Cambrer del senyor Rey**: The Royal Chamberlain (*Cambrer*), a significant household office with financial responsibilities. The reference to concessions (*concessions*) suggests grants of office or revenue.

- **Affaro**: Likely related to customs duties or port fees (*alfòndec* or similar); the exact term is unclear.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431)**: Queen consort of Aragon, wife of Joan I "el Caçador." She was daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Known for her cultural patronage and political influence. At this date (April 1395) she was seeking prayers for a male heir—their only surviving child was the Infanta Violant (later Queen of Naples).

**Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396)**: The reigning king at this document's date. He would die in May 1396 without male issue, and the crown passed to his brother Martí I.

**Guillem Ferrera**: Royal procurator (tax collector/administrator) for the City and Camp of Tarragona. The "Camp de Tarragona" was the agricultural hinterland administered with the city.

### Institutions

**Scala Dei (Cartoixa de Santa Maria d'Escaladei)**: Founded 1194, the first Carthusian monastery in the Iberian Peninsula, located in the Priorat region. It held significant royal patronage and was a site of spiritual importance to the Crown of Aragon. The queen's request for prayers for a male heir reflects the dynasty's anxious political situation.

### Context

The repeated concern for a male heir ("que placia a nostre senyor deus quens vulle donar fill") reflects the succession crisis. Joan I and Violant had lost multiple children; their daughter Violant was their sole surviving offspring. The lack of a male heir would lead to the succession of Martí I (1396) and eventually the Compromise of Caspe (1412).

These documents date from a critical period:

- **Franco-Aragonese relations**: The correspondence with Charles VI reflects the close dynastic and political ties between the courts.

### Script Analysis
The hand is a typical **cursiva gótica formata** of the Crown of Aragon chancery, c. 1390s. Features include:
- Looped ascenders on **d**, **l**, **b**
- The characteristic Catalan **ç** with cedilla
- Fusion of letters in common combinations (**st**, **ct**)
- Consistent use of the **p** with crossed descender for **per/par/pre**

### Abbreviation System
- **Nasal suspension**: tilde over vowels (mã = man, nre = nostre)
- **Superscript letters**: moˢ = mossèn, dña = domna
- **Standard sigla**: q̃ = que, p̄ = pre/per/par
- **Conventional suspensions**: -nt, -ment, -ció

### Date Format
The dating formula "M. ccc. xc v" (Gemini read as ".oz. cm xx v") represents the standard Roman numeral format for 1395:
- M = 1000
- ccc = 300  
- xc = 90
- v = 5

The apparent "oz" reading likely resulted from misreading of "M" with surrounding punctuation marks.

### Legal/Financial Terms

**Comanda**: A deposit or commenda—a sum of money entrusted to another party, often for safekeeping or investment. The failure to return a comanda was a serious legal matter requiring ecclesiastical or royal intervention.

**Procurador general**: A general procurator was a royally-appointed legal representative with broad powers to act on behalf of the Crown in judicial and administrative matters.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396):** Known as "el Caçador" (the Hunter) or "l'Amador de la gentilesa" (Lover of elegance). These documents date from the final months of his reign; he died on 19 May 1396 during a hunting accident at Foixà—**only days before Document 1's stated date**. This raises questions: either the dating requires reconsideration, or these are posthumous copies of earlier mandates, or the May date reflects registration rather than issuance.

**Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431):** Queen consort, niece of Charles V of France. Known patron of arts and culture. Joint issuance "lo Rey e la Reyna" reflects her active role in governance.

**Gabriel Cardona:** Vice-chancellor of the Crown of Aragon, documented in office during Joan I's reign.

**Paschal de Palo:** "Mestre de fusta dels palaus" – master carpenter/timber overseer for royal construction projects. Likely a master builder of some standing.

**Anthonius de Fonte:** Chancery scribe (escrivà de manament).

### Places

**Monastery of Sant Jeroni:** Almost certainly refers to the Hieronymite monastery project. In 1393, Joan I and Violant founded Sant Jeroni de la Vall d'Hebron (later relocated to become Sant Jeroni de la Murtra). The reference to "lo Priorat de la dita Ciutat" suggests the Vall d'Hebron foundation.

**Benifassà (Benifaçà):** Cistercian monastery of Santa Maria de Benifassà in the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit mountains (modern Castellón province). Founded 1233, it held extensive forests. The monastery's woodlands were famous for quality pine timber.

**Morella:** Important town in the Maestrat region, head of a community of aldeas (villages). The surrounding forests, including those associated with Benifassà, were under complex jurisdictional arrangements between the monastery and the municipality.

**Drassana/Daraçana:** The Royal Shipyards (Drassanes Reials) of Barcelona, major construction project of the 14th century, requiring vast quantities of timber for both construction and shipbuilding.

### Historical Context

These documents illuminate the resource demands of major royal construction projects in late 14th-century Barcelona. The Crown's simultaneous work on the royal palaces, shipyards, and a new monastery required negotiation with both ecclesiastical (Benifassà) and municipal (Morella) authorities for timber rights. The letters demonstrate the diplomatic formula of requesting (preguam) rather than commanding, while implicitly threatening to purchase elsewhere—a characteristic blend of royal prerogative and practical negotiation.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (1365–1431):** Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). In August 1386, Joan I was still Infante; he became king upon the death of Pere IV (Pere III of Catalonia) on 5 January 1387. This letter thus dates from the final months before Violant became queen regnant's consort. She maintained active diplomatic correspondence and was known for her cultural interests.

**Abū Fāris 'Abd al-'Azīz (Buçe):** Son of Abū Ḥammū II Mūsā (Boammo), Sultan of the Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen (r. 1359–1389). The Zayyanids ruled over western Algeria from their capital at Tlemcen and maintained complex diplomatic and commercial relations with the Crown of Aragon.

**Abū Ḥammū II (Boammo, d. 1389):** Zayyanid sultan, here titled "King of Tlemcen and of the Blessed" (Rey de Trimice e de benabenturat), a diplomatic rendering of his Arabic honorifics.

**Bernat Promotor:** The notary or secretary who drafted this letter by royal mandate. "Promotor" may be his surname or an office designation.

### Places

**Torroella de Montgrí:** Town in the Empordà region of Catalonia, where the royal household was residing when this letter was issued. The use of the "secret seal" (segell secret) indicates a less formal document than those issued under the royal majesty seal.

**Tlemcen (Trimice):** Capital of the Zayyanid kingdom in what is now northwestern Algeria. A major trading partner with Catalan merchants.

**Tarragona:** Major city in Catalonia; reference to hostages being held there relates to debt enforcement practices.

### Subjects

**The Giraffe and Cats of Aneta:** This letter provides fascinating evidence of exotic animal diplomacy between the Crown of Aragon and North African rulers. The "atzaraffa" (from Arabic *zarāfa*) is unambiguously a giraffe. The "Gats de aneta" likely refers to exotic felines—possibly serval cats or other African wildcats—identified as being "of Aneta" (possibly a place name or type designation). Such diplomatic gifts of exotic animals were prized in medieval European courts.

**Grain Export:** The request to allow a shipload of grain (*nauada de forment*) to be exported reflects the ongoing grain trade between North Africa and the Crown of Aragon, which was subject to periodic embargoes and required diplomatic authorization.

**Hostage Arrangements (Document B):** The reference to "hostages" (*hostatges*) relates to medieval debt enforcement practices whereby guarantors or their representatives could be detained until debts were satisfied—a form of surety rather than hostage-taking in the modern sense.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolanda of Bar), Queen of Aragon (c. 1365–1431)**
Wife of Joan I of Aragon, who died unexpectedly on 19 May 1396 during a hunting accident. The signature "La trista e dolorosa" (the sad and grieving one) reflects her mourning status, but also her precarious political position: she was pregnant at the time of Joan's death (later miscarrying), and the succession passed to Joan's brother Martí I. Violant spent much of her widowhood in legal disputes over her dower lands and in advocacy for her daughters' interests.

**Pope Benedict XIII (Pedro de Luna, c. 1328–1423)**
Aragonese pope of the Avignon obedience, elected 28 September 1394. The Crown of Aragon was his most consistent supporter during the Western Schism. These letters date from the early period of his pontificate, when the Aragonese crown was consolidating its support and seeking papal favor.

**Frater Nicolau de Costa**
Queen Violant's confessor, a master in sacred theology who served as her diplomatic envoy to the papal court. The use of confessors as diplomatic intermediaries was common practice in late medieval royal households.

**Frater Ongarcius de Guanebo**
A religious and master in theology who served as co-emissary with Nicolau de Costa. The name "Ongarcius" (Ungarico/Hongarès) may indicate Hungarian origin or connection. His role as oral messenger for matters too sensitive for written communication was typical of medieval diplomacy.

**Guillaume de Vergy, Cardinal (d. 1407)**
Created cardinal-priest of Santa Anastasia by Clement VII in 1391. Member of a prominent Burgundian noble family. His correspondence with Queen Violant suggests he was among the Avignon cardinals sympathetic to the Aragonese crown's interests.

### Context

These letters were written approximately thirteen months after Joan I's death and during a delicate period for the queen. The letter to the Pope concerns a papal rescript (formal written response) that has brought consolation regarding her grief—likely related to spiritual matters, masses for the king's soul, or possibly political assurances about her position. The use of oral messengers for sensitive matters (Brother Ongarcius) suggests there were diplomatic matters too delicate for the written record.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Document 1

**Date correction**: The date is definitively 1397, not 1387. Joan I of Aragon died on **19 May 1396** in a hunting accident at Foixà. The queen's reference to "la mort del senyor Rey senyor e marit nostre" (the death of the lord King, our lord and husband) confirms she is writing as a recent widow. The self-designation "la trista e dolorosa Reyna" (the sad and grieving Queen) is consistent with mourning correspondence.

**Violant de Bar** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon (1387–1396) as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. After Joan's death, she faced significant political marginalization under the new king, Martí I (Joan's brother). Her correspondence from this period shows efforts to maintain alliances and protect her position.

**The Countess of Urgell**: Almost certainly **Margarida de Montferrat** (d. 1418), wife of **Pere II, Count of Urgell** (r. 1347–1408). Pere was a grandson of Alfons III of Aragon and thus a kinsman of both Joan I and Violant. The "gran deute de consanguinitat" (great bond of consanguinity) referenced in the letter reflects this royal connection. The Urgell line would later contest the succession in the Compromise of Caspe (1412).

**"Segell secret"**: The use of the secret seal (as opposed to the great seal) indicates this was personal correspondence rather than official state business, appropriate for a condolence letter.

---

### Document 2

**Pere/Azcó Desplugues**: The Desplugues (or Esplugues) family were prominent Catalan nobles. A "camarlenc" (chamberlain) held one of the most intimate positions in the royal household. The petition concerns ecclesiastical benefices that had been granted through royal patronage.

**Church of Tortosa (Dertusa)**: The diocese of Tortosa, in southern Catalonia. The canonry and treasury (thesauraria) were significant benefices.

**Joan de Prades**: Likely a member of the **House of Prades**, a cadet branch of the royal house of Aragon. The counts of Prades were influential in ecclesiastical and court circles.

**Stephanus la Boria / auditor Sacri Palacii**: Reference to an auditor of the Roman Rota or Apostolic Palace, indicating this dispute had reached papal jurisdiction.

**Pope**: Given the date (1396–1397) and the Crown of Aragon's allegiance during the Western Schism, this letter would be addressed to **Benedict XIII (Pedro de Luna)**, the Avignon pope, to whom the Aragonese crown gave obedience.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Context and Significance
This letter was written **just over one month after the death of Joan I of Aragon** (d. 19 May 1396), who died without legitimate male heirs in a hunting accident at Foixà. Violant de Bar, his widow, writes to Pope Benedict XIII:

1. **Benedict XIII (Pedro de Luna)**: The Avignon pope, elected 28 September 1394. As a member of the powerful Luna family of Aragon, he had close ties to the Crown. Violant addresses him with the particular intimacy permitted by his Aragonese origins and their prior relationship.

2. **Joan I's Soul**: The letter is primarily concerned with securing spiritual suffrages (prayers, masses) for the soul of the deceased king—a standard queenly duty in the immediate aftermath of a royal death.

3. **Petrus Confessor/Camerarius**: The "Peter" mentioned appears to be a chaplain or confessor who served both the late king and the queen, now retained as *cambrerio* (chamberlain of the chapel or household). This may refer to a member of the royal chapel establishment.

4. **"Azarechus"**: This reading remains uncertain. It may be a personal name (possibly a Jewish or converso name?), or a place/title. Further research in related registers may clarify.

5. **"Pomp of this poor chapel"**: The language suggests financial difficulties in maintaining the royal chapel's obligations for memorial masses—consistent with the known fiscal crisis of the Crown at Joan I's death.

6. **The Postscript**: The Catalan autograph addition ("Molt car e molt amat pare e senyor jo he informat de ma part") suggests Violant added a personal note, possibly indicating she had sent a verbal message via an envoy in addition to the formal letter. The familiar address to Benedict XIII as "pare" reflects the language of spiritual kinship.

### Succession Crisis
Joan I's death triggered a contested succession resolved by the Compromise of Caspe (1412). His brother **Martí l'Humà** (Martin I) succeeded him, but this letter predates that resolution. Violant's concern for her late husband's spiritual welfare and the maintenance of the royal chapel reflects her immediate priorities as dowager queen.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolande de Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Following Joan's death on 19 May 1396, she was embroiled in succession disputes with her brother-in-law Martí I. These letters date from her early widowhood.

**Infanta Johana** (d. 6 August 1396): The youngest daughter of Joan I and Violant de Bar. Her death, announced here, occurred less than three months after her father's death. The succession crisis was acute because Joan I left no surviving male heirs.

**García Fernández de Heredia**: Archbishop of Zaragoza (1383–1411), a major ecclesiastical and political figure in the Crown of Aragon. Violant's use of a letter of credence suggests sensitive political negotiations.

**Charles III of Navarre** ("lo Rey de Nauarra") (1361–1425): Called "the Noble," he was Violant's first cousin (their mothers were sisters, both daughters of Jean II of France). The kinship term "cosi germa" (cousin-german/first cousin) reflects this relationship precisely.

**Francí de Bellcayre**: A member of Violant's household serving as butler (botellero), here acting as diplomatic envoy.

**Antoni**: A cook (coch) in Violant's service who had apparently entered the household of Charles III of Navarre—a minor but revealing detail about the movement of skilled servants between royal courts.

### Context

These documents date from a period of acute political uncertainty following Joan I's sudden death in a hunting accident (19 May 1396). Violant was pregnant at the time and hoped to secure the succession for a potential male heir. These August 1396 letters show her conducting diplomatic outreach while also dealing with personal tragedy (the death of her youngest daughter). The letter to Charles III reveals both the intimate tone of correspondence between royal cousins and practical household disputes.

**Critical correction**: Gemini dated these letters to 1376, reading the Roman numerals as "lxxvj." However, the manuscript clearly shows ".as. ccc xc vj" (1396). The numerals "as" represent "m" (1000) in this scribal convention, making the date M.CCC.XC.VI = 1396.

This dating is historically coherent: **Joan I of Aragon died on 19 May 1396** during a hunting accident at Foixà. These letters from Queen Violant, written in August 1396, express her grief as a widow ("la mort e priuacio de tan alt marit princep e senyor" - "the death and loss of so high a husband, prince, and lord").

The note "no fuy expedida" (not dispatched) indicates the first letter was superseded—likely by the second, expanded version that includes the credence clause for Francesc ça Garriga. This is standard chancery practice when a letter was revised before sending.

Mossèn Guillem, we have learned that our lord the Pope has said to diverse persons that he would give the Castellany of Amposta to the honest and religious Friar Pere de Vilafranca, Prior of Catalonia and Lieutenant General of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem in all Spain. Wherefore, Mossèn Guillem, we pray you that you be willing to make instance before the said lord Holy Father that he be willing to provide the said Friar Pere to the said Castellany. And additionally, if necessary, we pray you that you be his advocate for favors [intercessor] toward our cousin the King of France and Duke of Berry, of Burgundy, and of Bourbon, certifying you that [he is] already provided to the dignity and to the person sufficiently.
